case.case_title: Wickramasinghe v. Edmund Jayasinghe, Secretary, Ministry of Media, Tourism and Aviation

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the Emergency Regulations imposing censorship on publication of military-related news items violate the petitioner's right to equality before the law and equal protection under Article 12(1).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that the regulations impose a discriminatory 'blanket censorship' violating his fundamental rights under Article 12(1) by allowing some media to self-regulate while restricting his publication.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondent contended that the regulations are within the President's wide powers under the Public Security Ordinance, justified by national security concerns during a civil war, and that any differential treatment does not constitute unlawful discrimination.
key_facts: The petitioner is Chief Editor and Publisher of 'Janajaya' newspaper and ceased publication of military-related news due to regulations.
Emergency Regulations No. 1 of 1995 prohibit publication of certain military-related information.
Some state-controlled and foreign media were permitted self-regulation, but the Competent Authority retains power to act against any media.
The regulations were made under Section 5 of the Public Security Ordinance during a national crisis and ongoing civil war.
The petitioner alleges the regulations are unguided, vague, and discriminatory.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court recognized the wide discretionary power of the President to make regulations under the Public Security Ordinance in the interest of public security. It held that differential treatment of media does not necessarily amount to discrimination under Article 12(1) if the Competent Authority retains power to act against any media. The Court emphasized the context of national crisis and ongoing civil war as relevant to assessing the validity of the regulations.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the petitioner was not prevented from publishing his newspaper but chose to cease publication of military-related news. The Court held that the regulations were not a 'blanket censorship' but targeted sensitive information related to the war. The alleged preferential treatment to some media did not constitute unlawful discrimination as the Competent Authority's power was discretionary and not abdicated.
principles_established: Wide discretionary power of the President under Public Security Ordinance is subject to judicial review only on good grounds.
Differential treatment of media does not per se constitute discrimination if power to regulate remains.
Context of national security and ongoing civil war is critical in assessing restrictions on fundamental rights.
precedents_cited: Joseph Perera v. The Attorney General
Organisation for a Better Austin v. Kiefe

outcome.holding: The Court refused leave to proceed, holding that no prima facie case was made that the regulations violated Article 12(1) rights of the petitioner.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the petitioner's claim of unlawful discrimination in the application of censorship regulations. The Court's reasoning focused on whether the regulations violated the right to equality before the law and equal protection, making this clause dispositive.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court held that differential treatment of media does not per se constitute discrimination under Article 12(1) as the Competent Authority retains power to act against any media; the petitioner failed to show a prima facie violation of equality rights.
